<explanation>
Below is a tailored guide to help you, as a principal software engineer, draft a precise system-design diagram for FModel. FModel is a WPF desktop application (MVVM) that serves as an Unreal Engine archive explorer, relying on the CUE4Parse library for parsing UE4/UE5 assets. Use this advice to capture all essential components, their interactions, and the technologies involved.

1. Identify the Project Type and Purpose
   • Type: Single‐process desktop application built in C# with WPF (XAML + code‐behind).  
   • Purpose: Provide a graphical interface (Explorer) to browse, preview, convert, and “snoop” into Unreal Engine game archives, leveraging the CUE4Parse parsing engine.  

2. Analyze the File Structure
   • Presentation Layer (“FModel/Views” + “FModel/ViewModels”):  
     – Views: XAML files define UI controls, custom controls, and the 3D “Snooper” viewport.  
     – ViewModels: MVVM classes mediate data binding, commands, and user interactions.  
   • Application Services (“FModel/Services”):  
     – ApplicationService: central application lifecycle manager.  
     – DiscordService, other external API providers.  
   • Core/Domain Logic:  
     – Creator (packages, “Base…” classes) for exporting or customizing parsed assets.  
     – Extensions: helper methods for CUE4Parse, collections, clipboard, etc.  
     – Framework: command pattern, async queue, navigation, JSON serialization (JsonNetSerializer), logging (SerilogEnricher), ImGuiController for OpenGL.  
   • Settings and Persistence (“FModel/Settings”):  
     – User directory, endpoints, versioning, custom directory settings.  
     – Stored in local files/config.  
   • External Dependencies:  
     – CUE4Parse (submodule) for archive parsing.  
     – Newtonsoft.Json for JSON.  
     – Serilog for logging.  
     – OpenGL shaders and resources under “FModel/Resources.”  

3. Examine the README for Additional Insights
   • Core parsing library: CUE4Parse (external).  
   • Target platforms: UE4 & UE5 archives.  
   • Features: Asset preview, conversion, structural exploration, 3D model inspection.  

4. Components to Represent in the Diagram
   a. Presentation Layer  
      • WPF Views (XAML) ←→ ViewModel components  
      • Custom Controls (TreeView, AvalonEditor, 3D viewport)  
   b. Application Layer  
      • ViewModels dispatch Commands → Framework/Services  
      • Command Bus (ViewModelCommand → AsyncQueue)  
   c. Domain/Parsing Layer  
      • CUE4Parse Core Library  
      • Creator Package: Base classes for various game data (FN, BB, MV, SB)  
   d. Infrastructure Layer  
      • JSON Serializer (JsonNetSerializer)  
      • Logging (SerilogEnricher)  
      • ImGuiController + OpenGL Renderer (Shaders, Buffers) for 3D snooping  
   e. Persistence Layer  
      • Settings Manager (EndpointSettings, DirectorySettings) → Local files  
   f. External APIs  
      • Fortnite API, Epic API, GitHub API, FModel API, Valorant API (DynamicApiEndpoint classes)  
      • Discord integration  

5. Interactions & Data Flow
   • User clicks UI Control → Bound Command in ViewModel → passes through Framework to Service or CUE4Parse → Domain produces asset metadata or binary → returned to ViewModel → UI updates.  
   • 3D Model View (“Snooper”) → ViewModel triggers RenderLoop in ImGuiController → OpenGL buffers & shaders render UModel assets.  
   • Settings changes in UI → SettingsViewModel → SettingsManager writes to disk.  
   • API calls (GitHub, Fortnite) → FRestRequest → JSON deserialized via JsonNetSerializer → ViewModel displays results.  

6. Architectural Patterns & Design Principles
   • MVVM: clear separation of Views, ViewModels, and Models/Services.  
   • Command Pattern: Framework/Command classes encapsulate user actions.  
   • Dependency Injection (lightweight, manual): Services injected into ViewModels.  
   • Modular layering: Presentation → Application → Domain → Infrastructure → External.  
   • Submodule integration: CUE4Parse as black-box parsing engine.  

7. Diagram Guidelines
   • Layers: draw horizontal bands or concentric boxes for Presentation, Application, Domain, Infrastructure, External.  
   • Nodes:  
     – Presentation: Views, ViewModels  
     – Services: ApplicationService, DiscordService, ApiEndpoints  
     – Domain: CUE4Parse Parser, CreatorPackage  
     – Infrastructure: JsonNetSerializer, Serilog, ImGuiController  
     – Persistence: SettingsManager  
     – External: Unreal Archive files, REST APIs  
   • Connectors:  
     – Arrows indicating “calls,” “data flow,” or “binding.”  
     – Label arrows (e.g., “InvokeCommand,” “ParseArchive,” “DeserializeJSON,” “RenderFrame”).  
   • Annotations:  
     – Color-code by layer (e.g., Blue = Presentation, Green = Domain).  
     – Shapes: Rectangles for modules, cylinders for storage (settings files), cylinder or external icon for APIs.  
   • Detail level:  
     – Show key subcomponents (e.g., SnooperRenderer under Presentation).  
     – Group similar API endpoints under a single “API Endpoint Provider” node.  

8. Tailoring to This Desktop MVVM Project
   • Emphasize MVVM flow: UI ↔ ViewModel ↔ Services ↔ CUE4Parse.  
   • Highlight the “Snooper” 3D rendering pipeline (ImGuiController → OpenGL shaders/resources).  
   • Show Settings persistence and dynamic endpoint configuration.  
   • Depict how CreatorPackage classes extend the parsed data model for export.  

9. Essential Diagram Elements
   • Clear labels for every component.  
   • Directional arrows for exact data/control flow.  
   • Color coding to distinguish layers (e.g., Presentation = light blue, Domain = orange, Infrastructure = gray).  
   • Legends explaining shapes and colors.  

By following these steps and focusing on the MVVM layers, core parsing engine, service boundaries, and the 3D rendering pipeline, you’ll produce a system‐design diagram that fully captures FModel’s architecture in a clear, detailed, and actionable way.
</explanation>
